titre: The Great Vowel Shift in English
accroche: Bite, light, and night were already spelled with an i pronounced “ee,” as in ski. Today it's pronounced “eye,” and that's no exception.
contenu_vulgarise:
Bite, light, night, mice: when the spelling of these words settled, in the late Middle Ages, their i was pronounced like the i in *ski*. Today that same i is pronounced “eye,” as a diphthong. English spelling may seem capricious, but here it follows a precise logic: it photographs a pronunciation that then kept changing beneath it, without anyone touching it up.

## A Chain, Not an Isolated Accident

Between roughly the 15th and 17th centuries, all of English's long vowels shifted in the mouth, and did so as a linked set: each close-mid vowel (the long *e* of *meet*, the *o* of *boat* or *coat*) moves up a notch toward the position the close vowel just above it had held until then, “ee” and “oo” respectively. This chain movement, in which each vowel that rises pushes the next to rise in turn, has a name in historical linguistics: a push chain. The two vowels that were already the closest have nowhere to go: they split into diphthongs. That is what happens to the i of *bite*, *wife*, or *knight*, which becomes “eye,” and to the *ou* of *house*, which becomes “ow.” The Danish linguist Otto Jespersen was the first to describe this mechanism as a whole: in the first volume of his historical grammar of English, published in 1909, he devoted an entire chapter to it, titled “the great vowel-shift,” which gave the phenomenon its name.

## A Spelling Frozen Mid-Motion

This shift took several generations to stabilize. Yet it was precisely at that time, in 1476, that William Caxton set up the first printing press in England and undertook, to produce books readable by everyone, to fix a common spelling based on his own dialect, while pronunciation was still in the middle of change. The printers who succeeded him perpetuated these choices. The result: by the time the vowel shift ended, in the 17th century, spelling no longer moved. It keeps the trace of a vanished state of the language (an i that records an old “ee” become “eye,” an *ou* that records an old “oo” become “ow”).

So no original inconsistency explains why English is written one way and pronounced another. It is a precisely datable desynchronization: spelling never lied; it stopped being updated at the exact moment the spoken language took off.

repere.texte: The Danish linguist Otto Jespersen described and named the phenomenon in the first volume of his historical grammar of English, published in 1909, in a chapter titled “the great vowel-shift.” The change runs from roughly the 15th to the 17th century: exactly the period when English spelling was being fixed with the arrival of printing, in 1476.
repere.source: Otto Jespersen, A Modern English Grammar on Historical Principles, Part I, 1909

carte.punch: Bite was once pronounced “beet,” and now it's “bite”: the spelling never moved.
carte.idee: Between the 15th and 17th centuries, all of English's long vowels changed sound in a chain: bite, house, wife went from a simple sound to a diphthong. Printing, which arrived in 1476, fixed spelling in the middle of the movement, hence the mismatch that persists today.

quiz.question: Why does English spelling match current pronunciation so poorly, in words like bite or house?
choix: Because spelling was fixed with printing, in the 15th century, while the pronunciation of the long vowels was still changing, and it did not follow them afterward
Because English borrowed most of its spelling from French after the Norman Conquest, never adapting it to its own phonology
Because English dictionaries, unlike French ones, were never subject to official standardization
Because each English-speaking region kept its own local spelling, never unified nationwide
quiz.explication: Spelling was fixed with the arrival of William Caxton's printing press in 1476, in the middle of the Great Vowel Shift (15th-17th centuries): printers froze spellings that matched the pronunciation of the day, but the long vowels kept moving afterward, without spelling being touched up. Borrowing from French did influence English vocabulary, but doesn't explain this specific mismatch on long vowels; on the contrary, a de facto highly standardized spelling exists, born precisely of printing; and the phenomenon affects all varieties of English, not non-unified regional usages.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who first described and named this phenomenon of vowel change as a whole, and in which work?
choix: The Danish linguist Otto Jespersen, in 1909, in his historical grammar of English
The English printer William Caxton, in 1476, in his spelling manual
The English linguist Samuel Johnson, in 1755, in his dictionary
The American linguist Noam Chomsky, in 1965, in his syntactic theory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Otto Jespersen described and named the phenomenon, “the great vowel-shift,” in a chapter of the first volume of his historical grammar of English, published in 1909.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What becomes of the i in words like bite or night, at the end of the chain of vowel change, since it has nowhere further to rise?
choix: It drops a notch toward the position of the long e of meet
It splits into a diphthong, going from a simple sound to “eye”
It merges with the ou of house to form a single sound
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The two vowels that were already the closest, including the i of bite, have nowhere to rise: they split into diphthongs, “eye” for the i, “ow” for the ou of house.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does William Caxton do in 1476, at the very moment when English's long vowels are in the middle of changing?
choix: He translates the Bible into everyday English for the first time
He sets up the first printing press in England and fixes a common spelling
He writes the first complete dictionary of the English language
He bans the use of diphthongs in writing by royal decree
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1476, Caxton sets up the first printing press in England and, starting from his own dialect, fixes a common spelling, while pronunciation keeps changing beneath it.
